after:
The Dohkar’s accusation still rang when I found my voice. “It was not my doing. The girl took something I once told her in confidence and offered it to Fate on my behalf.”

The words left me thin. Every eye in the clearing pressed closer. The families who had come to witness their daughter’s First Sacrifice now stared at me as though the twist were my design. The youth knelt where the wish had taken her voice, hands at her throat, Weave-Script reduced to a single pale thread. She looked at me with the same startled hurt I felt.

A woman near the back—the one who had spoken the father’s name—stepped forward. “You broke the seal. You heard what you wanted and let the rite twist to serve yourself.”

“I broke the seal to stop the twist,” I said. My voice carried farther than I meant. “The sacrifice no longer matched the desire. If I had stayed silent the cost would have fallen worse than this.”

Julian stood at the edge of the circle. His heel had stopped its restless tap against the root. Slate-hued gray-green eyes flecked with brighter green held on me, and for one breath I felt the pull of them the way I always did when he looked at me like that—like he was already weighing whether I would choose the truth that hurt or the silence that protected what little standing I still had.

The Dohkar raised a hand. “The supervisor does not speak for the rite. She answers for it.”

Another voice rose from the families, sharp with fear for their own child’s future. “She let the girl pay for her own missing father. That is not guidance. That is theft.”

I felt the weight of their certainty settle. If I kept explaining I would only sound more guilty. If I stayed silent the youth would carry the full blame and my own past would remain untouched. The choice sat between my teeth like a stone I could not swallow and could not spit out.

The clearing waited. No one moved. Even the spiralgrass seemed to hold its breath.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out—"Petition Fate" is inscribed on it.

after:
The moss underfoot clung damp and alive, the stones beneath my bare soles slick with resurrection ivy. I hadn't meant to stop here—hadn't meant to breathe at all—but the families' bare feet scraped closer across the moss, hemming me in. The air pressed against my ribs with every accusation, the scent of crushed spiralgrass and old sweat rising from the ground. Every family had turned toward me now, the youth who had offered her silence still on her knees, her Weave-Script a pale thread against her aqua skin. The Dohkar's fingers were white-knuckled around the hilt of his ceremonial sash, his voice cutting through the quiet. "You broke the seal. You heard what you wanted and let the rite twist to serve yourself." His words cut deeper than the accusations already circling me.

I felt Julian before I saw him—his presence drawing my gaze toward the edge of the clearing before I chose to look. His slate-hued eyes found me, flecked with that brighter green near the irises, the one that always made the deck edges bite into my palm. He stood with his heels still, his frame cutting the last slant of light so the clearing dimmed by a shade. My fingers tightened around the old tarot deck in my lap, the gold leaf catching the dim light. The card that had slipped out—Petition Fate—pressed cold against my thigh, a reminder of the weight I'd placed on chance.

A woman near the back let out a sharp breath. "You let the girl's voice be taken for your own gain." She wasn't wrong. The truth hung in the air with the resin scent clinging to the Dohkar's sleeve—thick, undeniable. The youth's hands were still at her throat, her face slack with the loss of more than just her voice. I should have stopped the wish before it ever left her lips. I should have known she would take it, twist it, offer it to Fate on my behalf. The taboo wasn't just broken—it had shattered.

Julian's gaze didn't waver. His full lower lip, chapped and bitten, curled slightly at the corner. The way his head tilted—just a fraction—caught my attention where the band still tied across my mouth. I wanted to look away. I wanted to scream. But his attention held, keeping me rooted in the clearing's suffocating silence. My heel sank until cold mud squeezed between my toes, the damp seeping through the thin soles of my feet.

The Dohkar's voice rose again, sharper this time. "Silence is not an answer." His eyes flicked to Julian, then back to me. "The supervisor answers for the rite." The accusation settled in my stomach. I could feel the families' judgments pressing in, their whispers rising around me. One more word from me, and the suspicion would become certainty. One more breath, and the fragile story I'd built around my past would collapse under the weight of their stares.

I swallowed, the gossamer band still tied across my mouth suddenly too tight. The tarot deck in my hand felt heavier than it should have. Petition Fate stared up at me, its edges warm against my palm. The deck had leaned toward the choice I'd made earlier, just like it had every time I'd touched it. The cards had never been neutral. Neither was I.

She wasn't wrong. The truth hung in the air with the resin scent clinging to the Dohkar's sleeve—thick, undeniable. The youth's hands were still at her throat, her face slack with the loss of more than just her voice. I should have stopped the wish before it ever left her lips. I should have known she would take it, twist it, offer it to Fate on my behalf. The taboo wasn't just broken—it had shattered.

Julian's gaze didn't waver. His full lower lip, chapped and bitten, curled slightly at the corner. The way his head tilted—just a fraction—caught my attention where the band still tied across my mouth. I wanted to look away. I wanted to scream. But his attention held, keeping me rooted in the clearing's suffocating silence. My heel sank until cold mud squeezed between my toes, the damp seeping through the thin soles of my feet.

The Dohkar's voice rose again, sharper this time.

"Silence is not an answer."

His eyes flicked to Julian, then back to me.

"The supervisor answers for the rite."

The accusation settled in my stomach. I could feel the families' judgments pressing in, their whispers rising around me. One more word from me, and the suspicion would become certainty. One more breath, and the fragile story I'd built around my past would collapse under the weight of their stares.

I swallowed, the gossamer band still tied across my mouth suddenly too tight. The tarot deck in my hand felt heavier than it should have. Petition Fate stared up at me, its edges warm against my palm. The deck had leaned toward the choice I'd made earlier, just like it had every time I'd touched it. The cards had never been neutral. Neither was I.

I realize the deck is still in my hand. As I slide Petition Fate back in, I notice a flash of red in the otherwise gold stack.

"Tempt Fate."

Grandma never let me play with that one. A sword raised to a blood-red sky, lightning arcing down from the clouds (or maybe arcing up?) Ow! Static shock reminds me I need to pay attention to the present…
